title: Why Running AI Costs More Than Building It
subtitle: Training a large model is a one-time megaproject. Inference — actually answering your prompts — is the bill that never stops, and it's bottlenecked somewhere surprising.
hook: You'd think the expensive part of AI is *training* — the months of thousands of GPUs crunching the internet. That's a huge one-time cost. But for a model serving millions of users, the spending that dominates over its lifetime is **inference**: the compute burned every single time it generates a response. And the reason each answer is costly isn't what most people assume. It's rarely about raw math horsepower — it's about **memory bandwidth**.

sections.heading: Training once vs. answering forever
sections.body: Training is a fixed investment: run it, get a set of weights, done. **Inference** is what happens on every request, forever, for every user. A model like a large LLM might be trained once but then run *billions* of times. Multiply a few cents of GPU time by billions of calls and inference quietly becomes the larger line item — which is why AI companies obsess over shaving milliseconds off each token.

sections.heading: How an LLM actually generates text
sections.body:
An LLM writes **one token at a time** (a token ≈ a short chunk of a word). To produce each new token, it runs a full forward pass through the entire network, then feeds the result back in to produce the next one — an inherently **sequential** loop. You can't compute token #50 until you have token #49.

There are two phases. **Prefill** reads your whole prompt at once — highly parallel and efficient. **Decode** then generates the response token-by-token, and this is the slow, expensive part.

sections.label: The real bottleneck: memory bandwidth
sections.body: To generate each token, the GPU must read the model's **billions of weights** out of memory and into the compute cores — then do so *again* for the very next token. For single-stream decoding, the chips can multiply numbers far faster than they can fetch the weights to multiply. So the GPU spends much of its time *waiting for memory*, not computing. Inference is **memory-bandwidth bound**, which is why it can leave expensive compute cores idle.

sections.heading: What happens per token generated
items: Load the relevant model weights from GPU memory into the compute cores.
Run one forward pass over the current context to produce a probability distribution.
Pick the next token and append it to the output.
Update the **KV cache** — stored intermediate results so earlier tokens don't have to be recomputed. This cache *grows* with every token and eats memory.
Repeat for the next token. Longer outputs = more sequential steps = more cost.

sections.caption: Prefill digests the prompt in parallel; decode then loops one token at a time, re-reading weights and growing the KV cache each step.

sections.heading: How providers fight the cost
sections.body: Because the weights get read anyway, providers **batch** many users' requests together so each expensive memory read serves lots of people at once — the single biggest efficiency lever, though it trades off against latency. They also **quantize** models (store weights in 8- or 4-bit instead of 16-bit) to move less data, use smarter attention and KV-cache tricks, and route easy queries to smaller models. The economics are stark enough that a large slice of the AI industry's capital is now aimed not at training bigger models, but at making inference cheaper — because that's the cost that scales with success.

takeaways: Training is a one-time cost; **inference** recurs on every request and dominates over a model's life.
LLMs generate **one token at a time** in a sequential loop — that's inherently hard to speed up.
The bottleneck is usually **memory bandwidth**, not compute: the GPU waits to fetch weights.
The **KV cache** avoids recomputation but grows with every token and consumes memory.
Providers cut costs via **batching**, **quantization**, and cache tricks — inference efficiency is where much of the industry's money now goes.
